eras.label: The Reform Diets
eras.blurb: The Diet of Hungary met when the Habsburg emperor summoned it and was elected by the counties, which meant by the nobility. What the period lacks in franchise it makes up in consequence: these are the assemblies of Széchenyi and Kossuth, where the Hungarian language replaced Latin and serfdom was argued out of existence. The election of 1848 was the first held on anything resembling a modern register, and the revolution it belonged to was crushed within eighteen months.

eras.label: Dualism
eras.blurb: The Compromise of 1867 gave Hungary its own parliament inside the Habsburg monarchy, and the parliament spent fifty years arguing about the Compromise. A property and tax franchise kept the electorate to roughly six per cent of the population, voting outside the towns was open rather than secret, and the Liberal Party won every election but two. The one it lost, in 1905, produced a constitutional crisis the crown resolved by appointing a government the chamber had rejected.

eras.label: The Horthy era
eras.blurb: Hungary emerged from war, revolution and Trianon as a kingdom without a king, governed by an admiral without a navy. Elections continued, on a franchise that was secret in Budapest and open in the countryside, and the government party won all six of them. The last, in 1939, brought the Arrow Cross into parliament with the third largest vote.

eras.label: Between the armies
eras.blurb: The Provisional National Assembly of 1944 was assembled at public meetings in Soviet-held territory. The 1945 election that followed was the freest Hungary had ever held and was won outright by the Smallholders with 57%, which the Communists answered by carving the state up anyway. By 1947 the Communists were running the interior ministry and the count, and the election is remembered by the blue ballot papers that let their supporters vote in constituencies where they did not live.

eras.label: One list
eras.blurb: Nine elections in thirty-six years, none of them contests. Voters were handed a single list from the People's Front and asked to approve it; approval ran between 96 and 99% and turnout was reported above 94% every time. From 1966 a constituency could in principle field two candidates from the same front, which changed the seating plan and nothing else.

eras.label: The third republic
eras.blurb: Free elections returned in March 1990 and immediately produced the pattern that held for twenty years: every governing party lost the next election. A mixed system of constituency seats, county lists and a national compensation list gave majorities to whoever came first, and power alternated between the Socialists and Fidesz at every cycle but one.

eras.label: The two-thirds years
eras.blurb: The 2011 electoral law halved the chamber to 199 seats, dropped the second round, and added the winner's surplus constituency votes to its list total. Fidesz won three consecutive two-thirds majorities under it. In April 2026 the same system delivered 141 seats to Péter Magyar's Tisza Party on 53% of the list vote, which is the first time it has worked for somebody else.
